# Modeling {#sec-modeling}


Predictive modeling uses information available at a defined time to estimate
an outcome that is not yet known. This chapter asks whether fields available
when an illegal-parking request is created can help identify requests that
will remain open for at least one hour. We compare request detail and borough
with area context from the Census-linked table:


- population density;
- household vehicle availability; and
- median household income.


The analysis uses the same one-week, request-level data as earlier chapters.
It predicts recorded closure time; it does not show that area characteristics
cause a request to take longer or establish how predictions would perform in
a different week.


The one-hour outcome connects the modeling question to the operational
concern that illegal-parking reports may call for timely handling. It is an
analytical cutoff, not a documented agency response standard. In the
available week, 34.6% of requests with usable closure times were closed in
under an hour, while 65.4% remained open for at least an hour. Recorded
closure time is only a proxy for handling time: it may include dispatch,
travel, queueing, reporting, and administrative steps. The analysis can
predict this recorded outcome from observed fields, but it cannot isolate
those processes.


## Frame the Prediction


Before fitting a model, specify what it will predict and what information it
can use:


- **Unit:** one illegal-parking request from the distributed week.
- **Target:** one if recorded closure time is at least one hour, and zero
  otherwise. Requests without a closure time cannot be labeled and are
  excluded.
- **Prediction time:** request creation. Closure time and later processing
  fields are unavailable then and must not be predictors.
- **Request features:** problem detail and borough, recorded when the request
  is created.
- **Area features:** population density, median household income, and the
  estimated share of households with a vehicle, linked through the ZIP label
  [@census2024gazetteer; @census2024vehicles].


The one-hour cutoff is a modeling choice, not a documented agency standard.
The density measure divides ACS population by 2024 Gazetteer ZCTA land area;
the vehicle share is one minus the estimated fraction of households with no
vehicle. These describe area context, not curb capacity or individual
behavior. The ACS estimates cover 2020–2024, precede the request week, and
have sampling uncertainty. We do not calculate the vehicle share's
uncertainty from the published margins of error.


The ZIP label links a request to a ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA), but the
two geographies are related rather than identical, so this is an approximate
match [@census2023zip; @census2026american]. ZIP digits are labels, not
quantitative predictors. A later benchmark uses the ZIP as a category to
ask a different predictive question.


The prediction question is: among requests from this week, how well can the
recorded fields distinguish requests that remain open for at least an hour?
This is prediction within the observed setting. It is not a question about
whether a predictor causes a longer closure, nor does it show performance in
a future week. The four checks in @sec-formulation-checks still apply: a
model cannot repair an unclear target, an invalid measurement, an inadequate
scope, or weak evidence.


## Establish a Baseline


A baseline sets a reference that a more complex model must improve. Because
about two-thirds of eligible requests meet the one-hour target, predicting
the majority class for every request already gives roughly 65% accuracy.
That result does not distinguish requests: it labels every case as taking
at least an hour. Accuracy alone would therefore make a useless classifier
look respectable.


The analysis starts from the shared preparation function rather than
repeating the import and filtering workflow from @sec-wrangling. It links
the requests to the Census context already documented in
@sec-zcta-context-merge, reports unmatched and incomplete records, and
defines the binary outcome. It does not alter the source request data or
rebuild the Census lookup. The train-test split reserves one quarter of
complete requests for a final evaluation. Stratification keeps the target
proportion similar in the two sets; it does not make the records independent
or simulate a future week.


```{python}
from scripts.parking_requests import attach_zcta_context, load_parking_requests

import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

parking = load_parking_requests()
with_context = attach_zcta_context(parking)
matched = with_context["_merge"].eq("both")
has_income = with_context["median_household_income"].notna()
area_features = [
    "population_density_per_sqmi",
    "median_household_income",
    "share_households_with_vehicle",
]
has_area_context = with_context[area_features].notna().all(axis=1)
eligible = matched & has_area_context
required = [
    "closure_hours", "problem_detail", "borough",
    "incident_zip", *area_features,
]
model_data = with_context.loc[eligible, required + ["zcta"]].copy()
assert model_data[required].notna().all().all()
model_data["long_closure"] = model_data["closure_hours"].ge(1).astype("int8")
categorical_features = ["problem_detail", "borough"]
numeric_features = area_features
feature_columns = categorical_features + numeric_features + ["incident_zip"]
X = model_data[feature_columns].copy()
X[categorical_features] = X[categorical_features].astype("string")
X["incident_zip"] = X["incident_zip"].astype("string")
y = model_data["long_closure"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=2026, stratify=y
)

pd.Series({
    "requests in one-week extract": len(parking),
    "unmatched ZIP labels": int((~matched).sum()),
    "matched requests without income estimate": int((matched & ~has_income).sum()),
    "matched requests missing an area measure": int(
        (matched & ~has_area_context).sum()
    ),
    "eligible requests": len(model_data),
    "matched ZCTAs represented": model_data["zcta"].nunique(),
    "at least one hour": int(y.sum()),
    "under one hour": int(y.eq(0).sum()),
    "training requests": len(X_train),
    "test requests": len(X_test),
    "training target proportion": y_train.mean(),
    "test target proportion": y_test.mean(),
})
```


The checks make the analysis population and target visible before any model
is fitted. The lookup matches 13,033 of 13,040 requests; 58 matched requests
lack at least one area measure, including nine requests with no household
vehicle estimate because their ACS household denominator is zero. The
complete-case analysis therefore uses 12,975 requests from 176 ZCTAs. The
split contains 9,731 training requests and 3,244 test requests, with nearly
identical target proportions. Fixing
the random seed makes this example reproducible, while stratification
controls only the class proportions. Requests from the same ZCTA can appear
in both sets, so the test set evaluates new requests in areas represented
during training rather than transfer to unfamiliar areas.


## Use a GLM


A generalized linear model (GLM) relates a response distribution to a
predictor through a link function. For a binary outcome, the response is
modeled with a Bernoulli distribution and a logit link; this special case
is logistic regression. GLMs also include familiar linear regression with
a Gaussian response and identity link, as well as count models with a
Poisson response and log link. The response distribution and link should
follow the outcome's scale and support, rather than being selected only
because a software function is familiar [@nelder1972generalized;
@mccullagh1989generalized].


For request $i$, let $Y_i=1$ indicate that closure takes at least one
hour, and let $p_i = \Pr(Y_i=1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$. Logistic regression
models the log odds as a linear combination of predictors:


$$
\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik}.
$$


The inverse-logit transformation maps any real-valued linear predictor to
a probability between zero and one. Odds compare the probability of an event
with the probability it does not occur. For example, a probability of 0.75
corresponds to odds of $0.75/0.25=3$ to 1, while a probability of 0.5
corresponds to odds of 1 to 1. A coefficient describes a change in log odds,
holding the other included predictors fixed; exponentiating it gives an odds
ratio. An odds ratio is not a probability difference and does not by itself
describe a causal effect.


The first GLM includes problem detail, borough, population density, median
household income, and household vehicle availability. The three area
measures are standardized across training requests, so their odds ratios
describe a one-standard-deviation difference in the request-weighted
feature values.
The formula interface compares each categorical level with a reference
category and holds the other predictors fixed. These coefficients describe
conditional associations in the fitted model, not changes caused by the
area characteristics [@statsmodels2026generalized].


```{python}
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

glm_data = X_train.copy()
glm_data["long_closure"] = y_train
glm_formula = (
    "long_closure ~ C(problem_detail) + C(borough) + "
    "standardize(population_density_per_sqmi) + "
    "standardize(median_household_income) + "
    "standardize(share_households_with_vehicle)"
)
glm_fit = smf.glm(
    glm_formula,
    data=glm_data,
    family=sm.families.Binomial(),
).fit()

population_density_log_odds = glm_fit.params[
    "standardize(population_density_per_sqmi)"
]
income_log_odds = glm_fit.params["standardize(median_household_income)"]
vehicle_share_log_odds = glm_fit.params[
    "standardize(share_households_with_vehicle)"
]
pd.Series({
    "Population-density odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(
        population_density_log_odds
    ),
    "Income odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(income_log_odds),
    "Household vehicle-share odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(
        vehicle_share_log_odds
    ),
})
```


Each displayed odds ratio compares requests that differ by one training-set
standard deviation in the corresponding area measure, while the other model
features are held fixed. For example, an odds ratio above one indicates
higher fitted odds of a one-hour closure for a one-standard-deviation
increase; it does not say how many percentage points the probability rises.
The context values repeat across requests in the same ZCTA, so area patterns
are supported by 176 distinct ZCTAs, not by treating each request as an
independent area. These are conditional associations, not individual-level
effects or causal estimates. They also rely on a linear relationship between
each standardized area measure and log odds.


## Check the Model


Model checks ask whether the chosen specification represents the observed
relationships adequately. They differ from test-set evaluation: a model can
fit the training records poorly, or fit them closely while predicting new
records poorly. Logistic regression does not assume normally distributed
errors or constant error variance as ordinary least squares does. Its
assumptions instead concern the conditional Bernoulli response and the
specified relationship between predictors and log odds. Residual and
influence diagnostics can reveal unusual records or lack of fit, but no
single diagnostic proves that a model is correct [@hosmer2013applied;
@pregibon1981logistic].


The current model makes several assumptions that can be checked only in
part:


- Each standardized area measure has a linear relationship with log odds.
- The model is additive, so the detail contrast is the same across boroughs
  unless an interaction is included.
- Sparse categories may produce unstable estimates.
- Repeated Census values mean that area-level patterns are supported by 176
  distinct ZCTAs rather than by the full request count.


Compare observed outcome rates with mean fitted probabilities across
boroughs and across ordered groups of each continuous predictor, retaining
the count in each group. Calibration is one check: predictions near 0.7
should correspond to an observed outcome rate near 0.7 among comparable
requests [@vancalster2019calibration].


The training-set summary below compares observed target rates with average
fitted probabilities by borough. A large discrepancy can flag a lack of fit
for a group, while close averages do not rule out errors for individual
requests or interactions hidden within a borough. This is an in-sample check
for the simple GLM, not an estimate of future prediction accuracy.


```{python}
from IPython.display import display

glm_diagnostics = glm_data[["borough"]].copy()
glm_diagnostics["observed"] = y_train
glm_diagnostics["fitted"] = glm_fit.fittedvalues
display(glm_diagnostics.groupby("borough").agg(
    requests=("observed", "size"),
    observed_rate=("observed", "mean"),
    mean_fitted_probability=("fitted", "mean"),
))

for variable in numeric_features:
    check = glm_data[[variable]].copy()
    check["observed"] = y_train
    check["fitted"] = glm_fit.fittedvalues
    check["quintile"] = pd.qcut(check[variable], 5, duplicates="drop")
    display(check.groupby("quintile", observed=True).agg(
        requests=("observed", "size"),
        observed_rate=("observed", "mean"),
        mean_fitted_probability=("fitted", "mean"),
    ))
```


The evaluation section checks calibration for a fitted model. A calibration
plot groups predictions into bins and compares each bin's mean predicted
probability with its observed fraction. The diagonal marks perfect
calibration; binning is a summary, so it can conceal variation within a bin.


## Evaluate Predictions


Evaluation asks how well the fitted model predicts requests it did not use
for estimation or tuning. A training score is optimistic because the model
has already adapted to those records. The reserved test set is used only
after model choice; repeatedly adjusting a model after inspecting its test
performance turns that set into another training resource and weakens the
evaluation. Here, even a clean random holdout supports only a limited claim:
it estimates performance for additional requests drawn under a similar
one-week data-generating process.


Prediction metrics depend on the outcome's scale. Numeric outcomes are
evaluated by comparing predicted values with observed values; classification
begins with class probabilities and applies a threshold to assign labels.
The same train-test separation applies to both tasks, but their metrics answer
different questions.


### Numeric outcomes


For a numeric outcome, a residual is the observed value minus its prediction.
Three common scores summarize different aspects of these residuals:


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{MAE} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat{y}_i|, \\
\text{RMSE} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}, \\
R^2 &= 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
              {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Mean absolute error (MAE) reports a typical miss in the outcome's units.
Root mean squared error (RMSE) uses the same units but gives large errors
more influence because it squares them before averaging. The coefficient of
determination, $R^2$, compares squared prediction error with variation around
the observed mean; a test-set value can be negative when predictions are
worse than that reference [@scikitlearn2026metrics].


Recorded closure hours are numeric, so the held-out records also allow us to
compare simple duration baselines. The training mean is the constant
prediction that minimizes squared error; the training median minimizes
absolute error. This comparison shows how numeric prediction metrics work
without introducing a second fitted model.


```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

duration_train = model_data.loc[X_train.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_test = model_data.loc[X_test.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_scores = {}
for name, value in {
    "Training mean": duration_train.mean(),
    "Training median": duration_train.median(),
}.items():
    prediction = pd.Series(value, index=duration_test.index)
    duration_scores[name] = {
        "MAE (hours)": mean_absolute_error(duration_test, prediction),
        "RMSE (hours)": mean_squared_error(
            duration_test, prediction
        ) ** 0.5,
        "R-squared": r2_score(duration_test, prediction),
    }
display(pd.DataFrame(duration_scores).T)
```


The training-median baseline has lower MAE (2.67 hours) than the training-mean
baseline (3.16 hours), while the mean baseline has lower RMSE (4.96 hours
versus 5.25 hours). The right-skewed closure-time distribution lets a few
long closures have a large effect on RMSE. Both $R^2$ values are near zero or
negative, so these constant forecasts capture little of the test-set
variation. They provide reference errors, not an evaluation of a
feature-based regression model.


### Binary outcomes


For binary classification, a model often estimates a probability and then
uses a threshold to assign one of two labels. The positive class is the
category of interest, and changing the threshold changes the predicted
labels and the resulting threshold-based scores.


### Confusion matrix


A confusion matrix compares observed classes with the classes predicted at a
chosen threshold. Its four cells count correct and incorrect classifications.
A true positive (TP) is an actual positive predicted as positive; a false
negative (FN) is an actual positive predicted as negative. A false positive
(FP) is an actual negative predicted as positive; a true negative (TN) is an
actual negative predicted as negative. Rows below are actual classes and
columns are predicted classes, matching the convention used by scikit-learn
[@scikitlearn2026metrics].


| Actual class | Predicted positive | Predicted negative | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Positive | TP | FN | TP + FN |
| Negative | FP | TN | FP + TN |
| Total | TP + FP | FN + TN | $n$ |

: General layout of a binary confusion matrix. {#tbl-model-confusion-matrix}


In this chapter's parking analysis, a positive is a request that remains
open for at least one hour, and a negative closes sooner. The illustrative
threshold is 0.5, so predicted probabilities at or above 0.5 are classified
as positive. The displayed test-set counts use this rule and the layout in
@tbl-model-confusion-matrix.


Each metric uses a different margin or combination of cells. The numerator
and denominator make clear which errors a score counts:


| Quantity | Common names | Definition |
|:--|:--|:--|
| True positive rate | TPR, sensitivity, recall, hit rate, probability of detection | $TP/(TP+FN)$: fraction of actual positives flagged |
| False negative rate | FNR, miss rate | $FN/(TP+FN)$: fraction of actual positives missed |
| True negative rate | TNR, specificity, selectivity | $TN/(TN+FP)$: fraction of actual negatives not flagged |
| False positive rate | FPR, fall-out, false alarm rate | $FP/(TN+FP)$: fraction of actual negatives flagged |
| Positive predictive value | PPV, precision | $TP/(TP+FP)$: fraction of flagged requests that are positive |
| False discovery rate | FDR | $FP/(TP+FP)$: fraction of flagged requests that are negative |
| Negative predictive value | NPV | $TN/(TN+FN)$: fraction of unflagged requests that are negative |
| False omission rate | FOR | $FN/(TN+FN)$: fraction of unflagged requests that are positive |
| Accuracy | Overall accuracy, correct classification rate | $(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)$ |
| F1 score | F1 measure, F-score with $\beta=1$ | $2\,\mathrm{Precision}\,\mathrm{Recall}/(\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall})$ |


Different fields use different names for several of the same ratios:


- **TPR, sensitivity, and recall** all divide true positives by actual
  positives. They ask what fraction of requests that remained open at least
  an hour the model flagged.
- **PPV and precision** divide true positives by predicted positives. They
  ask what fraction of flagged requests remained open at least an hour.
- **Specificity and TNR** measure the fraction of actual negatives not
  flagged; **FPR** is the fraction of actual negatives that were flagged.
- **F1** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It does not account
  for true negatives.


The complementary pairs TPR/FNR, TNR/FPR, PPV/FDR, and NPV/FOR each sum to
one. The $F_\beta$ score makes the precision-recall balance explicit:


$$
F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2)
\frac{\mathrm{Precision}\,\mathrm{Recall}}
     {\beta^2\,\mathrm{Precision} + \mathrm{Recall}}.
$$


The familiar F1 score sets $\beta=1$. Values above one give more weight to
recall, while values below one give more weight to precision; the choice
should reflect the decision context rather than a universal preference
[@wikipediandevaluation; @scikitlearn2026metrics].


Accuracy is the fraction of correct labels and can hide poor performance on
one class when class frequencies differ. ROC AUC measures how well the model
ranks positive cases above negative cases across thresholds; 0.5 indicates
chance-level ranking and 1 indicates perfect ranking. AUC neither chooses a
threshold nor checks whether probabilities are accurate. Log loss evaluates
the probabilities themselves and penalizes confident errors. For observed
binary outcomes $y_i$ and predicted probabilities $p_i$, it is


$$
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
$$


These measures answer different questions and none is universally best
[@scikitlearn2026metrics].


The threshold determines how missed long closures trade off against
unnecessary alerts. The data do not specify the costs of these errors, so
the example uses 0.5 only for illustration. A threshold selected for use
would be chosen with training or validation data, then evaluated once on the
held-out test set.


The baseline assigns every request the training-set target prevalence as
its probability and predicts the majority class. The Census-context model
one-hot encodes problem detail and borough, standardizes the three area
measures, and fits logistic regression. The table compares their test
metrics; classification measures use a 0.5 threshold. Since the positive
class is more common, do not read accuracy alone. Compare it with ROC AUC,
log loss, and the confusion matrix to see whether the model finds requests
that close sooner or merely repeats the majority-class prediction.


```{python}
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    f1_score,
    log_loss,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    roc_auc_score,
)
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

candidate_features = categorical_features + numeric_features
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
    ("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
])
baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(
    X_train[candidate_features], y_train
)
baseline_probability = baseline.predict_proba(X_test[candidate_features])[:, 1]

model = make_pipeline(
    preprocessor,
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
)
model.fit(X_train[candidate_features], y_train)
test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test[candidate_features])[:, 1]

def score_predictions(probability):
    predicted_class = probability >= 0.5
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, predicted_class),
        "ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, probability),
        "log loss": log_loss(y_test, probability),
        "TPR / recall": recall_score(y_test, predicted_class),
        "specificity": recall_score(y_test, predicted_class, pos_label=0),
        "precision": precision_score(y_test, predicted_class),
        "F1": f1_score(y_test, predicted_class),
    }

from IPython.display import display

scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "Prevalence baseline": score_predictions(baseline_probability),
    "Census-context logistic model": score_predictions(test_probability),
}).T
confusion_table = pd.DataFrame(
    confusion_matrix(y_test, test_probability >= 0.5, labels=[1, 0]),
    index=["Actual at least one hour", "Actual under one hour"],
    columns=["Predicted at least one hour", "Predicted under one hour"],
)
display(confusion_table)
display(scores)
```


At the 0.5 threshold, the Census-context model has TPR 0.945, specificity
0.151, precision 0.678, and F1 0.790 on this test set. The prevalence
baseline flags every request as positive, so it has TPR 1, specificity 0,
precision 0.655, and F1 0.791. The context model identifies more negatives
while missing slightly more positives; its F1 is close to the baseline.
This comparison shows why no single score identifies a best model for every
use.


The calibration plot compares predicted probabilities with the observed
fraction for the preliminary model. A probability estimate of 0.7 should
correspond to an outcome rate near 0.7 among comparable predictions
[@vancalster2019calibration]. The points group held-out requests into
quantile bins, so the display can hide variation within each group.


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of held-out probabilities for requests taking at least one hour to close."
#| fig-format: svg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve

observed_rate, mean_probability = calibration_curve(
    y_test, test_probability, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile"
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="0.5", linestyle="--", label="Perfect calibration")
ax.plot(mean_probability, observed_rate, marker="o", label="Census-context model")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="Mean predicted probability",
       ylabel="Observed fraction meeting one-hour target")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```


The ROC curve traces the true positive rate against the false positive rate
as the probability threshold changes. In the table above, TPR is also called
recall or sensitivity; FPR is one minus specificity. Each point represents
a different threshold, so the curve displays the trade-off between finding
more one-hour closures and incorrectly flagging requests that close sooner.
The area under this curve is the ROC AUC reported in the score table.


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve for the preliminary Census-context model on held-out requests."
#| fig-format: svg
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

false_positive_rate, true_positive_rate, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_probability)
roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
ax.plot(
    false_positive_rate,
    true_positive_rate,
    label=f"Census context (AUC = {roc_auc:.3f})",
)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="0.5", linestyle="--", label="Chance ranking")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       ylabel="True positive rate (sensitivity / recall)")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```


This first comparison gives the model a common reference and an initial
held-out score. Its results are not the final model-selection result
because the regularization strength still needs to be chosen using training
data alone. A 0.5 classification threshold is convenient for illustration,
not a universal decision rule. A real alerting system would set a threshold
by considering the consequences of each kind of error with the people who
would use the predictions.


## Regularize Logistic Regression


The model has many coefficients because problem detail and borough are
one-hot encoded, and the later ZIP-label model adds a coefficient for each
observed area. Some categories are sparse, while the Census measures can be
correlated. An unpenalized fit can assign unstable, large coefficients to
these patterns and perform worse on new requests. Regularization limits
coefficient size to trade a small amount of training fit for more stable
predictions.


Logistic regression estimates coefficients by maximizing the Bernoulli
log-likelihood. A penalty adds a cost for large coefficients:


$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\lambda
= \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\left\{
-\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right]
+ \lambda P(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\right\}.
$$


Here, $p_i$ is the fitted probability for request $i$, and the penalty
does not include the intercept. The $L_2$ penalty is
$P(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2$; it shrinks coefficients
without usually setting them exactly to zero. The $L_1$ penalty is
$P(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|$ and can set some
coefficients to zero, producing a sparse model. Elastic net combines the
two penalties [@tibshirani1996regression; @zou2005regularization]. Since
several Census measures may carry overlapping information, this example
uses $L_2$ regularization to stabilize the estimates without arbitrarily
selecting one of a group of correlated predictors.


Scikit-learn's logistic regression applies $L_2$ regularization by
default. Its `C` parameter is inversely related to the penalty strength, so
smaller values apply stronger shrinkage [@scikitlearn2026logistic]. Numeric
predictors must be standardized because the penalty acts on coefficient
size; otherwise, a change in measurement units changes how strongly a
predictor is penalized. The analysis standardizes the area measures and
keeps preprocessing inside the cross-validation pipeline.


Cross-validation selects `C` using training data alone. Within each fold,
the pipeline learns its scaling, category encoding, and model coefficients
from the fold's training records, then evaluates log loss on its validation
records. The candidate with the lowest mean validation log loss is refitted
on the complete training set. The separate test set remains untouched until
selection is complete because using the same cross-validation scores both
to select and report final performance can be optimistic
[@scikitlearn2026crossvalidation; @varma2006bias].


The comparison separates measured area context from a postal-code lookup.
All four models use the same training and test requests. One model uses
problem detail and borough; a second adds three ACS-derived area measures;
a third adds the incident ZIP label as a categorical identifier; and a
fourth uses a smoothed target encoding of that label. Five-fold stratified
cross-validation selects `C` by log loss,
a probability-focused criterion. Standardization and one-hot encoding are
inside the pipeline so each fold learns its preprocessing from its own
training portion. The ZIP-label model is a predictive benchmark for areas
already represented in the data; its coefficient for a ZIP label does not
explain what neighborhood feature may relate to closure time.


One-hot encoding gives each ZIP label its own coefficient, which can be
unstable when some labels have few requests. Smoothed target encoding offers
another representation: it replaces a label with an estimate of its
one-hour closure rate, then shrinks that estimate toward the overall rate.
For ZCTA $j$, a common estimate is


$$
  \widetilde{p}_j =
  \frac{s_j + \alpha \bar{p}}{n_j + \alpha},
$$


where $s_j$ is the number of one-hour closures in ZCTA $j$, $n_j$ is
its number of requests, $\bar{p}$ is the overall training-set rate, and
$\alpha$ controls shrinkage. Larger values of $\alpha$ pull area
estimates more strongly toward the overall rate. This empirical Bayes idea
is useful for categories with different sample sizes
[@micci-barreca2001preprocessing; @pargent2022regularized]. Since the
encoding uses the outcome, fitting it on each row's own outcome would leak
information into the training data. The encoder below cross-fits the
training values within each training fold; for the held-out test set, it
uses category rates estimated from the full training set
[@scikitlearn2026targetencoder].


```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
candidate_C = {"logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}

def tune_logistic(categorical, numeric):
    transformers = []
    if categorical:
        transformers.append((
            "categorical",
            OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
            categorical,
        ))
    if numeric:
        transformers.append(("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric))
    encoder = ColumnTransformer(transformers)
    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        encoder,
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
    )
    search = GridSearchCV(
        pipeline,
        candidate_C,
        scoring="neg_log_loss",
        cv=cv,
        refit=True,
    )
    features = categorical + numeric
    search.fit(X_train[features], y_train)
    probability = search.predict_proba(X_test[features])[:, 1]
    return search, probability

zip_identifier_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
detail_borough_search, detail_borough_probability = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, []
)
census_search, census_probability = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, numeric_features
)
zip_id_search, zip_id_probability = tune_logistic(
    zip_identifier_features, []
)

zip_target_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    ColumnTransformer([
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
        (
            "zip_target",
            TargetEncoder(
                target_type="binary",
                cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026),
            ),
            ["incident_zip"],
        ),
    ]),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
)
zip_target_search = GridSearchCV(
    zip_target_pipeline,
    {
        "columntransformer__zip_target__smooth": [1, 10, 100],
        "logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10],
    },
    scoring="neg_log_loss",
    cv=cv,
    refit=True,
)
zip_target_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
zip_target_search.fit(X_train[zip_target_features], y_train)
zip_target_probability = zip_target_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[zip_target_features]
)[:, 1]

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Detail and borough": score_predictions(detail_borough_probability),
    "Census area context": score_predictions(census_probability),
    "ZIP label identifier": score_predictions(zip_id_probability),
    "ZIP target encoding": score_predictions(zip_target_probability),
}).T
comparison["selected C"] = [
    detail_borough_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    census_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_id_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_target_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
]
comparison["mean CV log loss"] = [
    -detail_borough_search.best_score_,
    -census_search.best_score_,
    -zip_id_search.best_score_,
    -zip_target_search.best_score_,
]
comparison["selected ZIP smoothing"] = [
    None,
    None,
    None,
    zip_target_search.best_params_["columntransformer__zip_target__smooth"],
]
comparison
```


For this split, adding the Census measures changes test ROC AUC from about
0.577 to 0.589 and log loss from 0.636 to 0.631. The improvement is modest,
but it indicates that the supplied area attributes add some predictive
information beyond problem detail and borough in this test design. The
ZIP-label model scores higher, with ROC AUC about 0.690 and log loss 0.593.
Because the same ZCTAs occur in training and test sets, this score reflects
area-specific prediction for locations represented in training. It neither
identifies a cause nor demonstrates transfer to a new ZCTA or a later week.


Smoothed target encoding gives a similar test ROC AUC of about 0.688 and
log loss of 0.595, with the cross-validation procedure selecting a smoothing
value of 10. Three test requests have ZIP labels absent from the training
set; the encoder assigns those labels the overall training rate. This
comparison shows that a compact, partially pooled encoding can retain much
of the ZIP-specific predictive signal in this split. It does not establish
that ZIP-level outcome rates will transfer to future requests, and its
learned category values should not be interpreted as neighborhood causes.


The Census estimates offer a more interpretable area-level question than
the ZIP label, but they do not measure the mechanisms that directly govern
parking or request processing. Population density is residents per square
mile, not curb or parking-space density. Household vehicle availability is
not ownership, registration, vehicle activity, or parking location, and
median household income does not describe an individual requester. These
ACS measures repeat across requests in the same ZCTA and carry sampling
uncertainty; the vehicle share's uncertainty has not been propagated. Only
176 ZCTAs contribute independent area contexts in this analysis. Direct
measures of curb regulations, parking supply, vehicle activity, or precinct
workload would be more informative for those processes. Any resource-
allocation use would also require a separate review of measurement, fairness,
and consequences for affected neighborhoods.


Regularization controls model complexity but does not replace diagnosis.
The selected penalty can stabilize estimates while leaving omitted
variables, measurement error, unfair performance differences, and domain
changes unresolved. Area-level predictors also require validation that
respects their shared geography when the intended use concerns new areas.
The model's intended use and validation design must therefore be considered
together.


## Exercises {.unnumbered}

These exercises extend the target definition and EDA in @exr-eda-time into
prediction. Use the same one-week extract and report eligible counts,
excluded records, the prediction time, and the features available then.
Treat closure time as a recorded duration, not a direct measure of officer
response.

::: {#exr-model-target}
Use closure of at least one hour as the binary target.

a. Report the counts and proportions below one hour and at least one hour.
   Compare them with the two-hour classification in @exr-eda-time and
   explain how changing the cutoff changes the prediction question.
b. Identify which fields are available when a request is created. Use the
   documented Census lookup to attach population density, median household
   income, and household vehicle availability through the incident ZIP label.
   Report unmatched requests and missing area estimates. Explain why the ZIP
   label is a join key rather than a numeric predictor, and state one
   limitation of the ZIP-to-ZCTA match or an area-level proxy.
c. Write one operational use for a prediction and identify who would act
   on it. State the cost of a missed request and a false alert that would
   need to be known before setting a decision threshold.
:::

::: {#exr-model-check}
Fit and assess a logistic model for the one-hour target.

a. Establish a majority-class or prevalence baseline. Split the records
   into training and test sets before fitting; state the split method and
   random seed.
b. Fit a model with problem detail and borough, then add the two Census
   area measures. Use cross-validation within the training data to select
   regularization strength. Report test ROC AUC, log loss, TPR, precision,
   F1, and a confusion matrix at a stated threshold. As a separate benchmark,
   fit a model that treats ZIP as a categorical identifier and explain what
   its score can and cannot tell you.
c. Make a calibration plot and inspect predicted performance by borough.
   Report group counts and describe one limitation of those comparisons.
   Compare request-random validation with a validation split grouped by
   ZCTA. Explain how the target use determines which split is more
   appropriate and what evidence from another week would be needed before
   claiming transfer to future requests.
:::
